clue.text: Given or taken away as corporal punishment

definitions.text: Given or taken away as corporal
definitions.meaning: first meaning: the chevron on the sleeve that marks an army rank, awarded on promotion and removed on demotion
second meaning: one blow of a whip or cane, an old word for a lash

explanation.surface: A soldier is promoted or demoted, and the phrase corporal punishment hovers over the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'corporal punishment' reads as one phrase, but the clue splits it: corporal is the army rank, and punishment stands alone.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a sleeve badge marking military rank and a single stroke delivered by whip or cane.

clue.text: Thus parson ordered some boys out of choir

parts.note: so is a synonym of thus

indicators.note: ordered means put into a new order, so the word beside it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A vicar sends some of the choirboys out of the church.
explanation.walkthrough: The parson looks like the man giving orders; in fact his name is the raw material being shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Boys with unbroken voices sing the highest part in a church choir, the treble or top line.

clue.text: Changed position, or renamed without one

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one word stands around the other

parts.note: OCR misread, flagged loudly: the scan shows renamed, but the printed word must be rested, took a break; the mend is one letter over the limit for filing it
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Someone either moved about or sat still, all alone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like lacking; here it is the old sense outside, so the letter sits within the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To resite something is to move it to a new location, so a building relocated has shifted place.

clue.text: Royal distinction from French university

parts.note: a prince is a member of a royal family
ton, borrowed from French, means style or fashionable distinction, as in bon ton
the French origin points to the borrowed word

explanation.surface: An award of royal honour arrives from a French source.
explanation.definitionFit: Princeton is a famous Ivy League university in New Jersey, in the United States.

clue.text: Was prepared to believe it could be done!

definitions.meaning: first meaning: took a statement as true

definitions.note: describes a thing as permissible: an accepted practice
definitions.meaning: second meaning: generally approved, the done thing

explanation.surface: Someone is persuaded that a feat really is possible.
explanation.definitionFit: The past tense means took something as true, and the adjective means sanctioned by custom, the done thing.

clue.text: Surface appearance of Orwell's book

definitions.meaning: first meaning: rising to the top of the water to breathe

explanation.surface: A critic remarks on the outward look of a George Orwell volume.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Surface appearance' sounds like a superficial look; it is a swimmer or whale reaching the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A diver or whale surfacing is literally rising to breathe, and the phrase is also the title of an Orwell novel.

clue.text: Joint measure on scale required in rising distress

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another
in a down clue rising means read from bottom to top, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: woe is grief or distress
lb is the abbreviation for a pound, a weight read on scales

explanation.surface: A worried person needs a reading on the scales.
explanation.definitionFit: The elbow is the hinge joint in the middle of the arm, between upper arm and forearm.

clue.text: Writer finds the gold conceals its colour

indicators.note: to conceal is to hide inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
or is gold as a colour in heraldry
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that gold hides its true colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Gold appears twice: once as the metal, Au, and once as its heraldic colour, or, which hides inside THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry David Thoreau was the American author of Walden, an essayist and naturalist.

clue.text: Ruler singled out from Hardy's work

indicators.note: singled means made singular, so the plural ending is dropped from the title

parts.note: The Dynasts is Thomas Hardy's verse drama of the Napoleonic wars

explanation.surface: A sovereign is picked out from a novel by Thomas Hardy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singled out' seems to mean chosen; here it means made singular, dropping the S of the title.
explanation.definitionFit: A dynast is a hereditary monarch, one member of a ruling family line.

clue.text: Larger group, of moderates, we hear? Not at all

definitions.text: Larger group, of moderates, we hear? Not at all

parts.words: Larger group, of moderates, we hear?
parts.note: surface reading: someone reports the moderates are the bigger faction
setter's reading: the bigger faction is one we never hear from, because it keeps quiet

explanation.surface: A rumour that the moderates outnumber the extremists is flatly denied.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we hear?' poses as hearsay; the answer is that we hear nothing at all from them.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names the mass of ordinary voters thought to hold moderate views but rarely express them publicly.

clue.text: Hopelessness in writing — I fail to get record back

indicators.note: back says the whole string built so far is read from the end

parts.note: MS, manuscript, is something in writing
I miss means I fail to hit
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A despairing writer fails to get a record released.
explanation.walkthrough: MS + I MISS + EP, all read backwards. 'Hopelessness in writing' tempts as a phrase, but 'in writing' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Pessimism is the gloomy expectation that things will turn out badly, a lack of hope.

clue.text: Rugby hero gets four points, going in at the corner

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Tom, hero of Tom ... Schooldays, set at Rugby School

definitions.text: gets four points, going in at the corner
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the snooker ball worth four points, potted in a pocket

explanation.surface: A rugby star scores a try out wide, in the days when a try counted four.
explanation.walkthrough: The rugby picture is a decoy for snooker, a cue game where the brown ball scores four when sunk in a pocket. Rugby School is an English public school.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom is the schoolboy hero of a Victorian novel about Rugby School, and the snooker ball scores four when sunk.

clue.text: One of his staff having sort of tack a head of embassy needed?

indicators.note: sort of says the next word is only loosely matched, a looser synonym is wanted

parts.note: to tack something on is to fasten or join it

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: An ambassador's aide with some kind of fastening, and an embassy chief who needs one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'his' points at the head of embassy later in the clue, so the definition leans on the wordplay's words.
explanation.definitionFit: An attache is a junior diplomat posted to an ambassador's staff at an embassy.

clue.text: Originality of various points

wordplay.note: seven compass points in turn: north, east, west, north, east, south, south

explanation.surface: Fresh ideas are found in several places at once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various points' sounds like assorted ideas; it is seven compass letters strung together.
explanation.definitionFit: Being original means being novel, fresh and not seen before.

clue.text: Rumour I don't spread

indicators.note: spread suggests the letters are scattered and laid out afresh

parts.note: the letters of these words, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Someone insists they never pass on gossip.
explanation.definitionFit: On dit, French for 'they say', is a piece of hearsay or gossip passed around.

clue.text: Few rhymes are so dependable

parts.note: surface reading: not many rhymes can be relied upon
setter's reading: two words that each rhyme with few

explanation.surface: A poet grumbles that rhymes rarely come out reliably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Few rhymes' looks like a scarcity complaint; read it as words that rhyme with few, and two of them form the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes someone staunchly loyal, especially a committed Conservative, steadfast and trustworthy.

clue.text: Promise to make both alter?

indicators.note: make asks us to form something new out of the letters that follow

parts.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A pledge meant to change two people's lives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alter' is part of the raw letters, though it looks like the instruction; the altar pun on marriage adds to the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A betrothal is an engagement, a formal pledge to marry.

clue.text: Parisian fortress as HQ until captured

indicators.note: something captured is held inside its captor

parts.note: a base is a headquarters
till is a synonym of until

explanation.surface: A Paris stronghold serves as headquarters until it falls.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface matches history: the fortress was stormed by a Paris crowd in July 1789.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bastille was the royal prison fortress in Paris stormed at the start of the French Revolution.

clue.text: In the fifties, an emblem of Welsh in Cardiff

definitions.note: a phrase for a place within the city, standing for its name

parts.note: L is the Roman numeral for fifty, so two of them are fifties
taken as written
daff is short for daffodil, a national emblem of Wales

explanation.surface: Back in the 1950s, a Welsh symbol could be seen around the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the fifties' looks like a decade; it is two Roman fifties.
explanation.definitionFit: Llandaff is a district of the Welsh capital, home to its cathedral.

clue.text: Clue, perhaps, about an originator of rebellion

definitions.text: Clue, perhaps, about an originator of rebellion

indicators.note: the originator of a word is its first letter, which is added on
about means turned round, so the letters before it are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
if expresses something that may be so, like perhaps
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A puzzle hint concerns the one who started a revolt.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: Satan led the angels' rebellion against God.
explanation.definitionFit: In Christian tradition Lucifer, the fallen angel, led the first revolt in heaven.

clue.text: This opera Sardou's cast acted, initially

definitions.text: This opera Sardou's cast acted, initially

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so each word gives its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of these five words

explanation.surface: An opera whose story Sardou's company first performed on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: Puccini's opera is based on La Tosca, a play by Victorien Sardou, so the whole clue is the definition too.
explanation.definitionFit: Tosca is Puccini's opera adapted from Sardou's play written for Sarah Bernhardt.

clue.text: Figure about right for height

indicators.note: about means going around, so one piece is wrapped around another

parts.note: a statue is a sculpted figure
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A body shape is judged correct for someone's height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure' looks like the definition, meaning build; it is the sculpture, and height is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Stature means how tall a person stands, their natural bodily size.

clue.text: Peg — one end of which is put in place

indicators.note: put in places pieces inside a word

parts.note: a spot is a place
the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: an end is the final position, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: which refers back to the peg, so this is the end of peg

explanation.surface: A peg with one end that has to be pushed into position.
explanation.walkthrough: 'which' stands for the definition word, so its end is the last letter of Peg.
explanation.definitionFit: A spigot is a small peg or plug used to stop the vent hole of a cask.

clue.text: Constable so alternating with one as painter

indicators.note: with here means holding, so one piece carries another inside it

parts.note: PC, police constable
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
taken as written
surface padding that hints the two short words trade places in the order

explanation.surface: John Constable takes turns with another artist at the easel.
explanation.walkthrough: Constable is a painter too, which hides that he is a police constable; 'so alternating' means so and as swap places.
explanation.definitionFit: Pablo Picasso was the Spanish painter who co-founded Cubism.

clue.text: Cut in financial interest, auditor might conclude

indicators.note: an auditor is a listener, so we go by what a hearer takes in

parts.note: a stake is a share in a business

explanation.surface: An accountant reviews someone's reduced share of a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'auditor' poses as an accountant; here it means a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak is a thick slice of meat or fish, a cut from the butcher.

clue.text: Brazilian state diplomacy used 10 disperse mob

parts.note: Rio de Janeiro is a state of Brazil
tact is diplomatic delicacy

explanation.surface: A Brazilian government uses diplomacy to break up a crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: The Riot Act was a 1714 British law read aloud to order a crowd to go home.
explanation.definitionFit: Officials once read this statute to a crowd, legally obliging it to break up within the hour.

clue.text: Foreman's outright blunder

indicators.note: out means removed, so a letter leaves the word

parts.note: a gaffer is a foreman or boss
read as out plus right; R is the abbreviation for right, the letter taken away

explanation.surface: The foreman made an absolute howler.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outright' reads as one word meaning utter, but splits as out plus right.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaffe is an embarrassing social mistake or tactless remark.

clue.text: Inconsistent statement — about John's nationality?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a remark that contradicts itself without the speaker noticing

definitions.note: a cryptic hint: saying John Bull is Irish would be one
definitions.meaning: second meaning: John Bull, the symbol of England, given the wrong country

explanation.surface: Someone contradicts themselves when asked where John comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: John Bull is the cartoon figure who personifies England, so calling him Irish is itself a contradiction.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names a self-contradictory or ludicrously illogical remark, once stereotypically attributed to the Irish.

clue.text: Nation's leader imprisoned by country's jailers

indicators.note: something imprisoned is shut inside, so one piece sits within another

parts.note: Turkey's, the country with the possessive s

indicators.note: a leader comes first, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A national leader is locked up by a foreign country's prison guards.
explanation.definitionFit: Turnkey is an old word for a prison warder, the man who holds the keys to the cells.

clue.text: Do some asset-stripping to run church

parts.note: to flee is to run away
CE, the Church of England

explanation.surface: A corporate raider strips a company and then bolts to church.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece is to swindle someone out of their money, as a shearer strips a sheep of wool.
